chapter.title: Open with a promise

cards.body:
MIT professor Patrick Winston had a firm rule for the first minute of any talk: no jokes. His reason had nothing to do with taste, and it changes what your first 30 seconds are for.

On a hike, nobody tightens their boots because you said thanks for coming. They tighten them when you point up and tell them **what they'll see from the top**.
cards.simpler: Patrick Winston, a professor at MIT, had one firm rule for the first minute of any talk: no jokes. His reason wasn't about taste. It changes what your first 30 seconds are for. Think of a hike. Nobody tightens their boots because you said thanks for coming. They tighten them when you point up and tell them **what they'll see from the top**.

cards.prompt: It's 6:40am at the trailhead. Twelve sleepy friends, one thermos, nobody moving. Which first line gets boots on the trail?

options.text: "Thanks so much for getting up this early, I really appreciate it."
"By 9, we'll be eating breakfast above the clouds."
"Okay, so a bear walks into a campsite..."

whyNot.a: That's the thank-you, not the reason to climb: kind, but it gives nobody a reason to take a step.
whyNot.c: That's the warm-up joke, not the summit: it's about the bear, not what they'll get from climbing.

cards.reteach: People start moving when they can see what's in it for them. The line that works points at the top and says what's waiting there.

cards.title: Why not the joke
cards.body:
Winston's reason was practical: in the first minute, **people haven't arrived yet**. They're sliding phones into pockets, shuffling chairs, getting used to your voice. A joke told now lands on a room still finding its seat.

So spend those seconds on a *promise*: one sentence that tells people what they'll be able to do or know by the end. It's you at the trailhead, pointing at the summit.

A promise names a gain, not a topic. "Today I'll talk about budgets" is a trail sign. "In 5 minutes you'll know the one number to check before any big purchase" is the view.
cards.simpler: Winston's reason was practical: in the first minute, **people haven't arrived yet**. They're still putting phones away. A joke now lands on a room still sitting down. So use those seconds for a promise: one sentence saying what people can do by the end. Name a gain, not a topic. "Today I'll talk about budgets" is a trail sign. "In 5 minutes you'll know the one number to check before any big purchase" is the view.

cards.title: Priya's two openings
cards.body:
Priya has 5 minutes at Monday's team meeting to introduce a new expense app. Draft one: "Hi all, thanks for having me, so, um, I'll walk you through the new expense tool." Three people quietly open their email.

Draft two: "By the end of this, **you'll file an expense from your phone before the taxi drops you off**." Same app, same 5 minutes. This time the person who lost a receipt last month looks up from their laptop.
cards.simpler: Priya has 5 minutes at Monday's team meeting to introduce a new expense app. Her first try: "Hi all, thanks for having me, so, um, I'll walk you through the new expense tool." Three people open their email. Her second try: "By the end of this, **you'll file an expense from your phone before the taxi drops you off**." Same app, same 5 minutes. Now the person who lost a receipt last month looks up from their laptop.

cards.prompt: Sam has 5 minutes at book club to get everyone reading one short story a week. Which opening points at the summit?

options.text: "Thanks, everyone. I know we're all busy, so I'll be quick."
"In five minutes you'll have a way to finish 52 stories this year without dropping a single novel."
"The short story goes back a long way, so let's start at the beginning."

whyNot.a: That's the polite warm-up, not the promise: it says the talk will be short, not what they'll gain.
whyNot.c: That's starting up the path before showing the summit: it names a topic, not a gain.

cards.reteach: In the first 30 seconds, everyone is quietly asking: what's in this for me? The opening that names something they'll have by the end answers it.

cards.title: Where the thank-you goes
cards.body:
You'd think the opening is the easy bit you write last. It's the opposite: **write the promise first**, because it's your summit said out loud. If you can't finish "By the end, you'll be able to...", you haven't picked the summit yet.

The thank-you doesn't vanish. It moves to one breath after the promise, or to the end, when people are glad they came.

Then keep the promise. People hold it like a folded map and check it at every bend. Promise 3 tricks and deliver 2, and the whole room notices the missing one.
cards.simpler: You might think the opening is the easy part you write last. It's the other way round: **write the promise first**. If you can't finish "By the end, you'll be able to...", you haven't picked your goal yet. The thank-you doesn't disappear. It moves to just after the promise, or to the end, when people are glad they came. Then keep the promise. People keep checking it. Promise 3 tricks and deliver 2, and everyone notices the missing one.

cards.body: Marco opens his quarterly update with a 40-second story about the office printer eating his slides. Half the room is still finding seats, and the punchline lands on the back of a latecomer's head. The test: if your first sentence could open anyone else's talk, it isn't a promise yet.
cards.simpler: Marco starts his quarterly update with a 40-second story about the office printer eating his slides. Half the room is still finding seats, and the punchline lands on the back of a latecomer's head. Here's a quick test: **if your first sentence could start anyone else's talk**, it isn't a promise yet.

cards.prompt: You're giving a 5-minute talk on sleep. Which first line is a promise?

options.text: "By the end, you'll know one thing to change at 10pm tonight to fall asleep sooner."
"I've been reading about sleep for six years."

whyNot.a: That's the trail sign, not the view: it names the topic but not what they'll gain.
whyNot.c: That's the guide's résumé, not the summit: it's about you, not what they'll be able to do.

cards.reteach: Ask of each line: does it tell the listener what they'll walk away with? A topic says where we're going and a credential says who's leading; only a promise says what they'll see from the top.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Your first 30 seconds aren't for warming up the room; they're for **pointing at the summit**. Tell people what they'll be able to do by the end, save the thank-you for later, then keep your word.

Tomorrow: the zigzag path two famous speeches secretly share.
cards.simpler: Your first 30 seconds aren't for warming up the room. They're for **pointing at the summit**. Tell people what they'll be able to do by the end. Save the thank-you for later. Then keep your word. Tomorrow: the zigzag path that two famous speeches secretly share.

cards.body: Pick something you'll explain this week, even how the washing machine works to a flatmate. Write one sentence starting "By the end of this, you'll be able to..." Say it out loud once.
cards.simpler: Pick something you'll explain to someone this week. It can be small, like how the washing machine works, told to a flatmate. Write one sentence that starts **"By the end of this, you'll be able to..."** Then say it out loud once.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write and say an opening line that tells the room what they'll gain from listening.
